"Frat" is simply a short, informal word for fraternity — a type of social club or brotherhood that exists at colleges and universities, mainly in the United States. Think of it as a close-knit group of male students who bond together, share a sense of belonging, and consider themselves "brothers."

A frat is an officially recognised student organisation at a college or university. Here is what makes it distinct:

  • It is for male students. (The female equivalent is called a sorority, not a frat.)
  • Members are called "brothers." The bond between members is described as brotherhood — a sense of loyalty, friendship, and shared identity, similar to a family.
  • It has a name made of Greek letters. Almost all fraternities are named using letters from the Greek alphabet, such as Sigma Chi, Delta Tau Delta, or Kappa Alpha. This is why fraternities and sororities are often collectively called "Greek organisations" or "Greek life."
  • Members typically live together. Most frats have a dedicated building on or near campus called a "frat house" (or fraternity house), where members eat, socialise, and often sleep.
  • Joining requires a process called pledging. You cannot simply walk in and become a member. New students go through a trial period called a "pledge period," during which they prove their dedication before being fully accepted.

A frat is not just a group of friends sharing a house. It functions like an organised institution with structure, traditions, and activities:

  • Social events and parties — Frats are widely known for throwing large, often loud parties. The phrase "frat party" is very commonly used to describe this.
  • Networking — Members build professional connections through the fraternity's alumni (former members), which can help them in their careers long after college.
  • Community service — Many frats engage in charity work or volunteer activities as part of their mission.
  • Academic support — Some frats maintain study resources or require members to meet minimum academic standards.
  • Rituals and traditions — Each frat has its own ceremonies, symbols, and traditions that create a shared identity and sense of pride.
The Informal Tone of the Word

This is important: "frat" is casual and informal. The proper, formal word is fraternity. When someone says "frat," it signals an everyday, conversational register — the way you'd speak with friends, not in an official document or formal speech.

Sometimes "frat" carries a slightly casual or even mildly dismissive tone depending on how it's used, almost as if someone is being a bit breezy about the topic. But in most cases, it is simply the common, shorthand way people refer to a fraternity in everyday conversation. You will almost never hear someone say "fraternity" in casual speech — "frat" is the dominant word in everyday usage.

You will frequently hear the phrase "frat boy" in American culture. This refers to a male college student who is a member of a frat — but over time, it has grown into a cultural stereotype. A "frat boy" is often stereotypically pictured as someone who:

  • Loves parties and socialising above all else
  • Is loud, rowdy, and sometimes reckless
  • Comes from a privileged or wealthy background
  • Prioritises social life over academics

It is crucial to understand that this is a stereotype, not a definition. Many frat members do not fit this image at all. The phrase "frat boy" is often used humorously, sometimes affectionately, and sometimes critically.

Frats are not without criticism. They have a complicated reputation in American society:

  • Hazing is perhaps the most serious issue associated with frats. Hazing refers to dangerous, humiliating, or abusive initiation rituals that older members sometimes inflict on new pledges. It has caused serious injuries and even deaths, and it is illegal in most US states, yet it continues to occur in some frats.
  • Exclusivity — Some frats have historically been associated with racial, religious, or class-based discrimination, though many organisations have worked to change this.
  • Alcohol culture — The association between frats and heavy drinking is strong and has led to many incidents on college campuses.

Despite all of this, many people who were in frats look back on the experience positively, citing lifelong friendships, personal growth, and professional benefits.

While "frat" almost always calls to mind the social kind described above, there are other types worth knowing:

  • Social fraternities — The classic kind. Focused on brotherhood, social life, and campus culture. This is what "frat" almost always means.
  • Professional fraternities — Organised around a particular career field (e.g., law, medicine, business). Less about parties, more about career development.
  • Honor fraternities — Based on academic achievement. You are invited to join because of your grades, not your social status. These are closer to academic clubs.
  • Service fraternities — Centred entirely around community service and volunteer work.

When someone says "frat" without any extra context, they almost certainly mean a social fraternity.

In short: a frat is a college brotherhood — an organised social group for male students, defined by shared traditions, a Greek-letter name, communal living, and a strong sense of loyalty between its members. The word itself is simply the everyday, informal way Americans refer to a fraternity.
